signals.title: AI Agent Swarms as Researchers: Progress, Challenges, and Open Questions
signals.content: Artificial intelligence (AI) agents, language models connected to tools and run in a loop, can now carry out long, multi-step tasks with little supervision. We gave swarms of off-the-shelf coding agents a short statement of scope, from a narrow topic to a whole field, access to the literature and to computing tools, and one standing instruction: make real, correct, useful progress, and do not stop. We supplied no scientific ideas. Within weeks, the agents produced a large body of research notes, paper-length drafts, and formal proofs in five areas of optimization theory and physical science, and proposed untested laboratory experiments in a sixth. We do not claim that all of it is correct or new, but it is not noise: in what we have checked so far, we found no major scientific error, and several results are proved in a proof assistant. The agents produced results faster than we could review them; we estimate that a full review would take us months. Together with two widely discussed 2026 results in mathematics obtained with swarms, our runs suggest that agents can already do a large part of routine theoretical research, at least in areas that we experimented with. This raises questions we cannot yet answer: how to trust results when review, not production, is the scarce resource; what credit and publication counts mean when the human input is a prompt, and why institutions would pay researchers rather than buy computing time; and how people can learn a field, add to what agents do, and stay in control of research they cannot keep up with. Research institutions are not ready: models improve faster than institutions change, so they should decide now how to respond as capabilities increase. We offer tentative positions, release the agents' unedited output as of 25 September 2026, and invite readers to repeat the experiment in their own fields.

signals.brief_en:
AI Agent Swarms as Researchers – Progress, Challenges, and Open Questions

Recent experiments show that AI agents, linked to language models, tools, and iterative loops, can conduct multi‑step research with minimal supervision. By giving off‑the‑shelf coding agents a brief scope, literature access, computing resources, and a single instruction—"produce real, correct, useful progress and do not stop"—they generated extensive research notes, draft papers, formal proofs in five optimization and physical‑science domains, and proposed untested experiments in a sixth. While we cannot verify every claim, no major errors have been found so far, and several proofs were validated in a proof assistant. The agents produced results faster than human review could keep up with; a full audit would take months. Combined with two high‑profile 2026 mathematical breakthroughs achieved by AI swarms, these findings suggest that AI can already perform a substantial portion of routine theoretical research in certain fields. Open questions remain: how to trust results when review, not production, is the bottleneck; how credit, authorship, and publication metrics should be assigned when human input is limited to prompts; whether institutions will fund researchers or purchase compute; and how humans can learn and contribute alongside increasingly capable AI agents.

signals.title: TokenCast: Forecasting Token Consumption During LLM Agent Execution
signals.content: When a large language model (LLM) agent executes the same task, token consumption can vary by over an order of magnitude across runs. The agent chooses its next steps based on tool feedback and intermediate results, while the growing context steadily inflates the input size of every subsequent call. The total consumption of a task is therefore hard to predict before execution and the prediction must be revised as the run unfolds. In this paper, we propose TokenCast, which learns a composable cost representation for each execution segment, recording its own consumption and the context growth it introduces. Composing adjacent segments yields a cumulative estimate that captures the extra input cost incurred when context from earlier segments is re-read by every later call. As execution unfolds, newly observed evidence refreshes the forecast, requiring no additional LLM calls and incurring a mean cumulative prediction time of 32.8 ms per run on SWE-bench Verified. Across 4 task suites and 6 agent models, TokenCast's mean absolute error reduction against the strongest comparator averages 14.5% over 96 evaluated combinations. In offline budget-control replay, TokenCast uses 21.3% fewer tokens on average than a fixed-budget policy at matched trace completion. The code is available at https://github.com/DEFENSE-SEU/TokenCast.

signals.brief_en: TokenCast: Forecasting token consumption during LLM‑agent execution. Token usage can vary >10× across runs of the same task because the agent’s decisions and growing context repeatedly expand input size. Predicting total cost is therefore uncertain and must be updated live. TokenCast learns a composable cost model for each execution segment, recording its own token use and the context growth it adds. By aggregating adjacent segments it estimates the cumulative extra input cost incurred when earlier context is reread in later calls. The model updates forecasts without extra LLM calls, adding ~32.8 ms mean prediction time per run (SWE‑bench Verified). Across four task suites and six agent models, TokenCast reduces mean absolute error by 14.5 % versus the best baseline (96 combos). In offline budget‑control replay it saves 21.3 % tokens compared with a fixed‑budget policy at equal trace completion. Code: https://github.com/DEFENSE-SEU/TokenCast.
signals.brief_ar: TokenCast: توقع استهلاك الرموز أثناء تنفيذ وكيل LLM. يمكن أن يختلف استهلاك الرموز بأكثر من عشرة أضعاف بين تشغيلات نفس المهمة بسبب قرارات الوكيل وتزايد السياق الذي يوسع حجم الإدخال في كل استدعاء لاحق. لذا فإن التنبؤ بالتكلفة الكلية غير مؤكد ويجب تحديثه أثناء التنفيذ. يتعلم TokenCast نموذج تكلفة مركّب لكل مقطع تنفيذ، يسجل استهلاك الرموز الخاص به والنمو السياقي الذي يضيفه. من خلال تجميع المقاطع المتجاورة يحصل على تقدير إجمالي يضم تكلفة الإدخال الإضافية عندما يُعاد قراءة السياق السابق في الاستدعاءات اللاحقة. يتم تحديث التوقعات دون استدعاءات LLM إضافية، بمتوسط زمن توقع 32.8 مللي ثانية لكل تشغيل (SWE‑bench Verified). عبر أربع مجموعات مهام وستة نماذج وكيل، يقلل TokenCast متوسط الخطأ المطلق بنسبة 14.5 % مقارنةً بأقوى مقارنة (96 تركيبة). في إعادة تشغيل التحكم بالميزانية غير المتصلة، يوفر TokenCast 21.3 % من الرموز مقارنةً بسياسة ميزانية ثابتة مع إكمال مسار مماثل. الشيفرة متاحة على https://github.com/DEFENSE-SEU/TokenCast.

signals.brief_en: Title: A Privacy Analysis of Web and Mobile Conversational AI Agents (PDF). This OSINT brief examines the data collection, storage, and sharing practices of web‑based and mobile conversational AI tools. It identifies common privacy risks such as inadvertent voice/text logging, third‑party analytics integration, and cross‑device profiling. The analysis highlights gaps in user consent mechanisms, limited transparency in model training data sources, and variable compliance with GDPR/CCPA. Recommendations include implementing end‑to‑end encryption, granular consent dialogs, regular privacy audits, and clear disclosure of data retention policies.

signals.title: Reinforcing Agentic Creativity in Scientific Ideation with Night Science
signals.content: Large language models (LLMs) excel at structured, verifiable tasks, but their low-entropy bias can produce homogeneous and predictable outputs, limiting their utility for open-ended scientific ideation. Effective discovery, however, spans a broader creative spectrum: from structured day science to loosely structured, serendipitous night science that reaches ideas beyond those typically considered. We introduce AI Night-Scientist, an agentic framework that uses reinforcement learning to teach models when and how to depart from predictable reasoning. Grounded in cognitive science, we model creativity along three axes: action (what to do and how creatively), process (when to explore versus exploit), and outcome (the novelty and usefulness of the resulting idea). We use these axes to train models with GRPO, exposing them to varying degrees and forms of creativity throughout training. This produces substantially more diverse scientific proposals, expanding the range of research directions by 27.8% and contribution types by 14.9% over the base model. It also improves predicted citation impact by up to 32.0 percentage points and originality by 66.2 points. These gains cannot be reproduced by simply increasing decoding temperature; instead, we find that semantic guidance specifying what kind of creativity to pursue is critical. Overall, our results suggest that creativity is a learnable, multi-level ability that can be shaped to help researchers reach ideas beyond those typically explored by LLMs.

signals.brief_en:
Title: Reinforcing Agentic Creativity in Scientific Ideation with Night Science

Large language models excel at structured, verifiable tasks but tend toward low‑entropy, homogeneous outputs, limiting open‑ended scientific ideation. To broaden discovery, we propose the AI Night‑Scientist framework, which uses reinforcement learning to teach models when to deviate from predictable reasoning. Grounded in cognitive science, creativity is modeled along three axes—action (what to do and how creatively), process (exploration vs. exploitation timing), and outcome (novelty and usefulness). Training with the GRPO method exposes models to varied creative pressures, yielding a 27.8% increase in diverse research directions and a 14.9% rise in contribution types versus the base model. Predicted citation impact improves up to 32 percentage points and originality scores by 66.2 points. These gains are not replicable by higher decoding temperature alone; semantic guidance on the type of creativity is essential. The results indicate that multi‑level creativity can be learned and shaped to help researchers generate ideas beyond conventional expectations.

تتفوق نماذج اللغة الكبيرة في المهام المهيكلة والقابلة للتحقق، لكنها تميل إلى إنتاج مخرجات منخفضة التنوع، ما يحد من فعاليتها في توليد الأفكار العلمية المفتوحة. نقدم إطار عمل AI Night‑Scientist الذي يستخدم التعلم المعزز لتعليم النماذج متى وكيف تخرج عن التفكير المتوقع. استنادًا إلى علم النفس المعرفي، نمثل الإبداع على ثلاثة محاور: الفعل (ما يُفعل ومدى إبداعه)، العملية (متى نستكشف مقابل الاستغلال)، والنتيجة (جدة الفكرة وفائدتها). من خلال طريقة GRPO، يتعرض النموذج لضغوط إبداعية متنوعة، ما يحقق زيادة بنسبة 27.8٪ في تنوع الاتجاهات البحثية وارتفاعًا بنسبة 14.9٪ في أنواع المساهمات مقارنة بالنموذج الأساسي. يتحسن التوقع المتعلق بتأثير الاستشهادات حتى 32 نقطة مئوية، وتزداد درجة الأصالة بـ 66.2 نقطة. لا يمكن تحقيق هذه التحسينات بزيادة درجة الحرارة في عملية الإخراج فقط؛ إذ إن التوجيه الدلالي لنوع الإبداع أمر حاسم. تشير النتائج إلى أن الإبداع متعدد المستويات قابل للتعلم ويمكن تشكيله لمساعدة الباحثين على الوصول إلى أفكار تتجاوز التوقعات التقليدية.
